overview: Silla began as the smallest of Korea's Three Kingdoms but eventually unified the peninsula through strategic alliances. Its unique bone-rank social system, gold crowns and Hwarang warrior youth organization reflect a distinctive civilization.

items.text: Gold crowns with tree and antler motifs found in royal tombs at Gyeongju.
Bulguksa Temple and Seokguram Grotto represent the pinnacle of Buddhist art.
Cheomseongdae observatory, one of the oldest surviving astronomical structures in Asia.
The bone-rank system determined social status and official positions by birth.
The Hwarang organization trained aristocratic young men in martial arts, Buddhism and Confucian ethics.
Buddhism officially adopted, leading to temple construction throughout the kingdom.
Gyeongju developed as a major capital with palaces, temples and markets.
Aristocratic culture emphasized refinement, poetry and Buddhist practice.
Gyeongju Historic Areas designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Unified Silla period created foundations for later Korean culture.

fall.text: The last Silla king Gyeongsun surrendered to Goryeo in 935, ending nearly a millennium of Silla rule.
